planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Timor Hybrid coffee is frost-tender and best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Discovered growing spontaneously on the island of Timor in the early twentieth century, this naturally occurring cross between Arabica and Robusta combines Arabica's cup quality with Robusta's resilience, carrying broad-spectrum resistance to coffee leaf rust and coffee berry disease that has made it the single most important disease-resistance donor in modern coffee breeding. Rather than being planted commercially on its own, it lives on mainly as the hidden ancestor behind rust-resistant cultivars like Catimor and Sarchimor, though pure Timor Hybrid plantings still persist in Timor-Leste's mountain forests. Give it the same warm, humid, filtered-shade conditions as other Arabica types, in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and expect a vigorous, disease-tolerant plant that shrugs off pressures that devastate less hardy varieties.
sources: World Coffee Research reference
CIRAD (Centre de Coopération Internationale en Recherche Agronomique pour le Développement) reference
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Yellow Bourbon coffee is frost-tender and best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: First noticed in the São Paulo town of Pederneiras around 1930, Yellow Bourbon arose from a natural cross or mutation involving red Bourbon coffee, and it ripens to a golden-yellow rather than the usual red, a trait that also seems to slow the fruit's sugar breakdown and lets growers pick over a longer harvest window. Brazilian growers quickly embraced it for combining Bourbon's celebrated sweetness and balance with noticeably heavier yields, and it remains a staple parent behind many later Brazilian cultivars. Grow it exactly as you would red Bourbon, in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil under filtered shade, with steady warmth and moisture and protection from frost.
sources: World Coffee Research reference
Instituto Agronômico de Campinas (IAC), Brazil
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Pink Bourbon coffee is frost-tender and best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: First identified among farms in Colombia's Huila department in the early 2010s, Pink Bourbon takes its name from the blushing peach-pink color of its ripe cherries, a hue that falls between the classic red and yellow Bourbon types and may reflect a natural hybrid origin rather than a simple color mutation. It has become a favorite of specialty coffee producers for cups showing pronounced florals and juicy stone-fruit sweetness, though yields are modest and mother trees are still relatively scarce outside a handful of Colombian growing regions. Cultivate it like other Bourbon-type Arabicas, with rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, filtered shade, and consistent moisture, and be patient waiting for wider availability of true-to-type plants.
sources: World Coffee Research reference
Federación Nacional de Cafeteros de Colombia (FNC)
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Wush Wush coffee is frost-tender and best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Named for the forested district of Wushwush in southwestern Ethiopia where it grew as an untamed local landrace, this heirloom Arabica was carried to South America in the 1990s and has since found a following among growers in Colombia and Panama chasing its unusually floral, fruit-driven cup, often compared to Geisha's. As with most Ethiopian landraces it is genetically variable rather than a single fixed clone, so performance and flavor can differ from planting to planting, and yields tend to run lower than modern commercial cultivars. Grow it at higher elevations under filtered shade in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and treat it as a connoisseur's planting rather than a high-volume producer.
sources: World Coffee Research reference
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Icatu coffee is frost-tender and best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Bred at Brazil's Instituto Agronômico de Campinas beginning in 1950 by crossing tetraploid Robusta with Arabica and repeatedly backcrossing the progeny to Mundo Novo over many generations, Icatu was the first successful artificial Arabica-Robusta hybrid released for commercial planting and takes its name from a Tupi-Guarani word evoking calm after a storm. It inherited useful disease and nematode tolerance from its Robusta ancestry while keeping recognizably Arabica-quality cups with notes of chocolate and light citrus, and it typically out-yields older Brazilian cultivars like Mundo Novo by a healthy margin. Grow it in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil under filtered shade with the same warm, frost-free conditions other Arabicas need, expecting a vigorous, tall-growing tree.
sources: Instituto Agronômico de Campinas (IAC), Brazil
World Coffee Research reference
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Obatã coffee is frost-tender and best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Developed at Brazil's Instituto Agronômico de Campinas from a cross between the breeding line IAC 1669-20 and Yellow Catuaí, Obatã combines a compact, dwarf growth habit with strong resistance to coffee leaf rust and consistently high cup quality, a combination that has made it popular with Brazilian growers looking to replace older, disease-prone cultivars. Its short stature allows closer spacing and easier hand harvesting than tall heirloom types, while its late maturation spreads out the picking season. Grow it in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil under filtered shade, giving it the same warm, frost-free care as other dwarf Arabica cultivars like Catuaí.
sources: Instituto Agronômico de Campinas (IAC), Brazil
World Coffee Research reference
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Laurina coffee is frost-tender and best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Arising as a natural mutation of Bourbon coffee on Réunion Island (once called Île Bourbon) sometime in the 18th or 19th century, Laurina is prized for beans containing roughly half the caffeine of ordinary Arabica along with a delicate, low-acid, distinctly sweet cup with notes of stone fruit and honey. Its narrow, pointed beans (giving rise to the alternate name Bourbon Pointu) come from a smaller, more slender, lower-yielding plant that is markedly harder to grow and harvest than standard Bourbon, which keeps it rare and sought after among specialty roasters. Provide the same rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil and filtered shade other Arabicas need, but expect slower growth and lighter harvests in exchange for its unusual low-caffeine cup.
sources: World Coffee Research reference
CIRAD (Centre de Coopération Internationale en Recherche Agronomique pour le Développement) reference
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; IMC 67 cacao is a frost-tender tropical tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Collected from a wild population on an island in the Amazon River near Iquitos, Peru during germplasm expeditions of the 1930s that formed the historic 'Pound collection,' IMC 67 (its name short for Iquitos Mixed Calabacillo) is a pure Upper Amazon Forastero type valued for strong resistance to witches'-broom, moniliasis, and black pod, along with early flowering and tolerance of periodic flooding. It has been used worldwide as breeding stock, most famously as one of the two parents of the high-yielding Ecuadorian clone CCN-51. Grow it like other cacao, in rich, moist, well-drained soil beneath taller shade trees, with steady warmth and humidity and protection from wind while young.
sources: International Cocoa Germplasm Database (ICGD), University of Reading
International Cocoa Organization (ICCO) reference
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; UF-613 cacao is a frost-tender tropical tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Selected in Costa Rica among the early twentieth-century United Fruit Company cacao trials, UF-613 became one of the most widely planted clones in Central America thanks to its large pods, good bean size, dependable disease tolerance, and strong yields. Recent genetic studies have found that it carries an unusually distinct ancestry compared to other Upper Amazon Forastero selections, suggesting it preserves lineage not well represented in most other commercial cacao. Cultivate it beneath taller shade trees in rich, moist, well-drained soil, providing the warm, humid, frost-free conditions cacao needs throughout the year.
sources: International Cocoa Germplasm Database (ICGD), University of Reading
CATIE (Tropical Agricultural Research and Higher Education Center), Costa Rica
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; Matina cacao is a frost-tender tropical tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Named for Costa Rica's Matina Valley on the Caribbean coast where it has been grown by smallholders for generations, Matina (formally the clone Matina 1-6) is today the most widely cultivated cacao type in the world, forming the backbone of Costa Rican and much of Central American cacao production thanks to its dependable yields and pleasant, well-balanced flavor. Its importance to the global crop made it the subject of one of the first complete cacao reference genomes sequenced by international researchers. Grow it beneath taller shade trees in rich, moist, well-drained soil, with the same warm, humid conditions and frost protection other cacao types require.
sources: CATIE (Tropical Agricultural Research and Higher Education Center), Costa Rica
International Cocoa Germplasm Database (ICGD), University of Reading
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products
